_notes: E4 R1.3: what the bishop's visit to a parish finds (systems/bishop/visits.ts). The letter is drawn from these pools by the parish record (its kind, its school, its debt, its people) and, when the visit finds it, the pastor's private struggle and hidden trait. Tokens: {parish}, {pastor}, {town}. Invented and flagged.

flagship_suburban: {parish} is what the diocese points to: a full parking lot, a school with a waiting list, a finance council that brings the audit to the dinner. {pastor} runs it like a man who expects to be moved and is not sure he minds.
The suburbs came to {parish} and stayed. Three Masses on Sunday, a youth minister with a budget, and a pastor who has learned to say no to the deanery because the parish says yes to everything.
struggling_urban: {parish} was built for two thousand families and has three hundred. The church is the finest in the diocese and the boiler is the oldest; {pastor} shows you both, in that order, and does not have to say what he wants.

The neighbourhood around {parish} changed twice since the church was built, and the parish changed once. {pastor} knows every one of the three hundred by name, which is the whole case for keeping it open.
immigrant_growing: {parish} has more people than pews on Sunday, in two languages, and the choir is the best you have heard in the diocese. {pastor} needs a second priest who speaks Spanish and asks for one in front of the whole council.
The Spanish Mass at {parish} fills the church and the hall; the English Mass has forty. {pastor} runs both and is tired in a way the parish does not see.
rural: {parish} is a church, a cemetery, a hall, and a town of nine hundred, an hour from the cathedral on a road that closes in February. The Mass is full because it is the only thing in town that is. {pastor} has three churches and one car.
At {parish} the confirmation class is six and the potluck is the whole town. {pastor} asks nothing of you and would like the roof looked at.
difficult: {parish} has been difficult for three bishops. The council is two families who do not speak, the school closed under your predecessor and nobody has forgiven him, and {pastor} has been there four years and looks it.
Nobody wanted {parish}, and {pastor} was sent. He has made something of it that the diocese has not noticed, and says so, once, at the door.

open: The school is full and the principal is the best administrator in the parish, including the pastor.
at_risk: The school has a hundred and forty children and needs two hundred to live, and the principal knows the number better than you do. She asks you, in front of the parents, what the diocese means to do.
closing: The school closes in June, and the visit is the first time the parents have seen the bishop since it was announced. They are polite. The parking lot is not.
none: There is no school, and the children of the parish go to the public one and to the religious education program on Wednesday nights, which is run by a woman who has done it for thirty years and would like a stipend.
The books balance, which in this diocese is a form of holiness.
some: The parish carries a debt it services and does not reduce; the finance council calls it manageable, in the tone of people who have decided not to look.
heavy: The debt is larger than the parish will ever pay from the plate, and the finance council has known it for years. Nobody says the word merger. Everybody hears it.

aging: The Sunday congregation is grey, kind, and thinning by a funeral a month.
mixed: The Sunday congregation is what a parish should be: children in the front pews and their grandparents behind them, and a crying room that is used.
young: The parish is young: strollers in the aisle, a baptism most Sundays, a pastor who has not slept since the school opened.

drink: In the rectory, after the dinner, {pastor} pours himself a third glass and does not notice that you have counted. The housekeeper has. The file had not.
doubt: Late, on the rectory porch, {pastor} says something about faith that a priest does not say to his bishop unless he has stopped being careful, and then is careful again.
loneliness: {pastor} keeps you talking until midnight, about nothing, and you understand on the drive home that he has nobody else to keep talking.
anger: A parishioner interrupts the dinner with a question about the Mass schedule, and {pastor} answers her in a voice you have not heard from him before and the parish has.
health: {pastor} takes the stairs to the choir loft one at a time, and stops on the landing, and says it is the knee, and it is not the knee.
family: {pastor}'s mother is in the rectory's back bedroom, and has been for two years, and the parish nurses her between the Masses. The file says he lives alone.
ambition: {pastor} asks about the chancery twice at dinner and once at the door, and shows you the parish as a man shows a house he means to sell.

fragile: {pastor} is holding something together with both hands, and the parish holds him.
careerist: {pastor} has read your priorities and preaches on them, and is watching to see whether you noticed.
mystic: {pastor} says Mass as if nobody were watching, and the parish watches him do it.
hiding_something: There is a room in the rectory {pastor} does not show you, and a subject he changes twice.
smarter_than_he_lets_on: {pastor} plays the country pastor for the visit and then, at the door, asks a question about the canon that the vicar general could not have.
loyal: {pastor} would take a bullet for the diocese and has taken several for the parish, and says nothing about either.
restless: {pastor} has been at {parish} four years and has already left, in the way that matters.

vacant: {parish} has no pastor: a retired priest from the next county drives in for the Sunday Mass and the deacon runs the rest. The people ask you the one question, and you give them the one answer, which is that you are looking.
again: They remember the last visit, and the promise you made at it, and ask about it at the door.
